newsitem.title: USA: NYC Independent Budget Office sees bigger gaps.
newsitem.headline: NYC Independent Budget Office sees bigger gaps.

text.p: The New York City Independent Budget Office (IBO) Friday forecast "significantly higher" budget gaps in fiscal years 1998 to 2001 than those projected by Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, in his financial plan.

The IBO estimated a gap of $701 million in the fiscal year budget for fiscal year 1998, which starts on July 1. The gaps would increase to $3.8 billion in 2001, which would be $1.3 billion above the mayor's forecast for that year.

In its latest report, the IBO explained that for fiscal year 1998 it lowered its estimate for revenues by $258 million, as it disagreed with whether the city would get as much back rent as it claims it is owed by the Port Authority, which leases its airports. The dispute is under arbitration.

Yet for tax revenues, the analysts were more optimistic, as they see $32 million of extra funds in fiscal 1998, and $48 million more in 1999, though the gains will be partly offset by tax cuts that may cost more than Giuliani estimated. The IBO was more gloomy about the future, projecting $39 million less revenue in 2000 and $248 million less in 2001.

Also, the IBO said expenditures would run $443 million higher in fiscal 1998, which includes an extra $103 million for bigger welfare costs due to sweeping changes in the federal program. The IBO said the mayor's underestimate of welfare spending would grow to $206 million by fiscal 2001.

However, the newly created IBO, which serves the same function for the city as the federal Congressional Budget Office, estimated New York City will get much more aid for education, public and medical assistance from the state than Giuliani forecast: $219 million more in fiscal 1998, and $598 million more by 2001. And the budget analysts look for Washington to contribute $550 million more aid than the mayor does in 1998, and up to $741 million more by 2001.
